claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles from single-source precursors is governed by inhibition of precursor atomic mobility during reduction.
Restricted precursor mobility promotes stochastic incorporation of diverse metal atoms into a single homogeneous phase.
A homogeneous HEA can form even when the constituent metals reduce consecutively rather than simultaneously.
The initial material is a homogeneous mixture of noble-metal single-source precursors containing at least five elements.
Additives can be used to inhibit atomic mobility during nanoparticle nucleation.
Changing the quenching rate can modulate atomic mobility during nanoparticle nucleation.
Atomic diffusion is kinetically limited under the proposed low-temperature reduction conditions.
Slower cooling or omission of mobility inhibitors increases atomic mobility.
Mobility inhibition leaves reduced atoms insufficient time to rearrange.
Atoms with limited mobility are captured randomly by growing nuclei, producing a homogeneous HEA.
Greater atomic mobility permits longer-range diffusion and thereby causes elemental segregation or phase separation.
Mobility-inhibited synthesis will produce single-phase HEA nanoparticles with homogeneous elemental distributions.
Mobility-enhanced synthesis will show more elemental segregation or phase separation than mobility-inhibited synthesis.
Standard single-source-precursor reduction conditions already yield single-phase HEA nanoparticles because they inherently limit mobility.
The mechanism applies to multimetal systems with at least five elements under low-temperature, fast-reduction conditions.
The mechanism may fail in binary or some ternary systems because those systems require cooperative reduction dynamics for phase uniformity.
No quantitative threshold for the mobility inhibition needed for successful HEA formation is established.
